title: Iron Deficiency Anemia: Find the Blood Loss
bottomLine: Iron deficiency is both a diagnosis and a clue. Replace iron, but also identify why iron was lost or not absorbed—especially occult gastrointestinal bleeding in adults and heavy menstrual bleeding in reproductive-age patients.
recognize: Microcytosis, low ferritin, fatigue, pica and restless legs can occur, but early iron deficiency may be normocytic.
differentiate: Thalassemia trait can cause microcytosis with relatively preserved RBC count and normal iron stores; inflammation can raise ferritin despite iron restriction.
assessment: Assess diet, heavy menses, pregnancy, GI symptoms or bleeding, blood donation, NSAID use, celiac risk and prior bariatric surgery.
workup: Use CBC and ferritin with inflammatory context; investigate gastrointestinal or gynecologic blood loss based on age, sex and risk rather than simply prescribing iron indefinitely.
management: Use oral iron when effective and tolerated; use IV iron when oral therapy is ineffective, poorly absorbed, not tolerated, or too slow for the clinical need.
medicationSafety: Iron commonly causes gastrointestinal adverse effects and is toxic in overdose, especially to children; counsel on safe storage.
redFlags: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult
counselling: Explain administration strategies, expected stool darkening and when gastrointestinal adverse effects warrant a different formulation or route.
followUp: Document hemoglobin response and repletion of iron stores, then close the loop on the cause.
examTrap: Treating iron deficiency in an older adult without evaluating occult blood loss.
oneLinePearl: Iron deficiency asks two questions: how do we replace it, and where did it go?
sourceBasis: Canadian gastroenterology and hematology practice resources

title: Macrocytosis: B12, Folate, Alcohol, Marrow, or Medication?
bottomLine: Macrocytosis is not synonymous with B12 deficiency. Check neurologic features, diet and malabsorption, alcohol, liver or thyroid disease, medications and marrow disease; treat B12 deficiency promptly when neurologic injury is possible.
recognize: B12 deficiency can cause paresthesias, gait change and cognitive symptoms even before severe anemia.
differentiate: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia but not the classic B12 neurologic syndrome; reticulocytosis can also raise MCV.
assessment: Assess vegan or restrictive diet, pernicious anemia risk, GI surgery, metformin or PPI exposure, alcohol use and neurologic symptoms.
workup: Use CBC and smear, B12, and targeted folate, TSH, liver and reticulocyte studies; methylmalonic acid can clarify selected borderline B12 results.
management: Replace B12 by oral or parenteral route according to cause and severity; address folate deficiency after B12 deficiency has been considered.
medicationSafety: Folate alone can correct anemia while allowing B12-related neurologic damage to progress.
counselling: Explain lifelong replacement when irreversible malabsorption or pernicious anemia is present.
followUp: Recheck hematologic response and neurologic recovery.
examTrap: Giving folate alone for macrocytosis before considering B12 deficiency.
oneLinePearl: Never let folate hide a B12 neurologic problem.

title: Hemolysis: Is the Marrow Keeping Up?
bottomLine: Hemolysis is suggested by anemia with reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, elevated LDH and low haptoglobin. The urgent question is whether hemolysis is immune, mechanical, infectious, inherited or microangiopathic.
recognize: Jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly and fatigue may occur.
differentiate: Thrombotic microangiopathy adds thrombocytopenia and organ injury; autoimmune hemolysis can have a positive direct antiglobulin test.
assessment: Ask about transfusion, medications, infection, autoimmune disease, prosthetic valves, pregnancy and family or ancestry-related inherited disease risk.
workup: Use CBC and smear, reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin and DAT; schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia requires urgent thrombotic microangiopathy assessment.
management: Stabilize severe anemia and treat the cause; suspected TTP is a hematologic emergency requiring immediate specialist treatment rather than waiting for every confirmatory test.
medicationSafety: Do not wait for the historical full pentad of TTP before escalating suspected microangiopathic hemolysis.
counselling: Explain triggers and recurrence risk for inherited or immune conditions when applicable.
followUp: Track hemoglobin and hemolysis markers through cause-specific care.
examTrap: Diagnosing iron deficiency from anemia alone when the smear and bilirubin indicate hemolysis.
oneLinePearl: Anemia plus high reticulocytes asks where the red cells are being lost or destroyed.

title: Thrombocytopenia: Bleeding Risk and Mechanism
bottomLine: First confirm the platelet count is real, then decide whether thrombocytopenia reflects decreased production, destruction or consumption, sequestration or dilution. Bleeding, neurologic or renal injury, pregnancy, thrombosis or heparin exposure raises urgency.
recognize: Petechiae and mucosal bleeding are typical of platelet disorders; spontaneous major bleeding risk rises as counts become very low, but the clinical context matters.
differentiate: Pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping should be excluded in a stable asymptomatic patient.
TTP, DIC, HIT and HELLP are time-critical causes.
assessment: Review infection, medications and heparin exposure, alcohol and liver disease, pregnancy, autoimmune disease, thrombosis and bleeding.
workup: Repeat count and smear, and obtain coagulation or hemolysis studies according to the phenotype; use a validated pre-test probability approach before HIT testing.
management: Treat the cause; obtain urgent hematology input for TTP, severe immune thrombocytopenia or unexplained profound thrombocytopenia; if HIT is sufficiently likely, stop heparin and follow a non-heparin anticoagulation pathway.
medicationSafety: Platelet transfusion is not routine treatment for TTP and may be harmful unless life-threatening bleeding or a compelling procedural indication exists.
counselling: Avoid NSAIDs and high-trauma activities when bleeding risk is clinically significant.
followUp: Trend platelets and ensure the diagnostic cause is resolved or appropriately followed.
examTrap: Ordering HIT antibody testing for every low platelet count without estimating clinical probability.
oneLinePearl: Confirm the count, then classify production versus destruction or consumption.

title: Febrile Neutropenia: Antibiotics Are Time-Critical
bottomLine: Fever with clinically important neutropenia after chemotherapy or marrow disease is an oncologic emergency. Obtain cultures promptly, but start appropriate broad antipseudomonal antibiotics without avoidable delay.
recognize: Inflammatory signs can be muted; sepsis may present with fever, malaise, hypotension or subtle localizing symptoms.
differentiate: Neutropenic fever may have no obvious source; absence of pus or leukocytosis does not reassure.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, line sites, mouth, lungs, abdomen and perianal symptoms, urinary symptoms and timing of recent anticancer therapy.
workup: Obtain CBC with differential, blood cultures from appropriate sites and targeted imaging or laboratory tests; avoid unnecessary rectal instrumentation when mucosal injury and bacteremia risk are concerns.
management: Use prompt empiric antipseudomonal antibiotics and a validated risk-based inpatient or outpatient oncology pathway; unstable patients require sepsis resuscitation.
medicationSafety: Do not delay antibiotics waiting for every result when a known high-risk treatment patient is clinically septic.
counselling: Patients receiving myelosuppressive therapy need exact instructions about what fever or symptoms require immediate contact.
followUp: Coordinate culture results and oncology-directed duration and growth-factor decisions.
examTrap: Giving acetaminophen and observing a febrile chemotherapy patient at home while waiting for next-day blood work.
oneLinePearl: Fever plus neutropenia is antibiotics now, source finding in parallel.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario and Canadian oncology febrile-neutropenia practice resources

title: Lymphadenopathy: Reactive Node or Malignancy Signal?
bottomLine: Most acute tender nodes are reactive, but persistent, hard or fixed, supraclavicular or generalized nodes with constitutional symptoms require a malignancy or systemic-disease workup.
recognize: Recent upper-respiratory, dental or skin infection and EBV commonly cause reactive adenopathy.
differentiate: Lymphoma often causes persistent painless adenopathy; metastatic nodes depend on drainage territory.
assessment: Assess duration, location, size, tenderness, fixation, generalized versus local distribution, fever, night sweats, weight loss, infection or exposure and medications.
workup: Use CBC and targeted infectious testing; ultrasound can characterize superficial nodes, but persistent suspicious adenopathy often needs tissue diagnosis rather than repeated imaging alone.
management: Treat a clear infection, observe low-risk reactive nodes with planned reassessment, and refer suspicious persistent adenopathy for biopsy.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric corticosteroids before tissue diagnosis when lymphoma is plausible because they can obscure pathology.
counselling: Provide a defined reassessment interval rather than telling the patient only to watch the node.
followUp: Document resolution or proceed to tissue diagnosis when the node persists or evolves.
examTrap: Giving steroids for unexplained persistent lymphadenopathy before biopsy.
oneLinePearl: Suspicious lymph nodes need tissue, not repeated steroid trials.
sourceBasis: Canadian oncology and hematology diagnostic principles
